items.title: Cristiano Ronaldo marries longtime love Georgina Rodríguez in Portugal
items.description: Cristiano Ronaldo is married! The Portuguese soccer star, 41, tied the knot with his longtime partner, model Georgina Rodríguez, in a civil ceremony on August 11, 2026, in Cascais, Portugal, according to a press release. The ceremony was a “private and intimate moment” attended by their five children. Ronaldo shared a photo of the couple’s hands with their wedding bands with the caption: “C G”. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Cristiano Ronaldo (@cristiano) The wedding comes one year after Rodríguez, 32, announced their engagement on Instagram on Aug. 11, 2025. For the announcement, she shared a picture of her hand over Ronaldo’s, offering a close-up look at her massive, oval-shaped diamond sparkler. “Sí, quiero. En esta y en todas mis vidas,” Rodríguez wrote in the caption, which translates to, “Yes, I do. In this and in all my lives.” The couple shares five children : twins Eva Maria and Mateo, 9, daughter Alana, 8, daughter Bella, 4, and 16-year-old son Cristiano Jr., whom Ronaldo welcomed in a previous relationship. Georgina Rodríguez shares a photo of her engagement ring Credit: Georgina Rodri­guez/instagram He and Rodríguez previously announced the death of Bella’s newborn twin brother, Ángel, in April 2022. Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodríguez with their kids. Credit: Cristiano Ronaldo/Instagram Ronaldo first met Rodríguez when she was working as a sales assistant at a Gucci store in 2017. That January, the two made their red carpet debut at the Best FIFA Football Awards in Zurich. By May, they made things Instagram official when Ronaldo posted a photo of himself and Rodríguez. In Rodríguez’s 2022 Netflix reality series, I Am Georgina , Ronaldo opened up about the early days of their romance . The athlete said he thought Rodríguez was a “very interesting girl, so much more mature for her age,” but that he didn’t expect the romance to last. Georgina Rodríguez and Cristiano Ronaldo share a kiss after a game in 2018. Credit: Alexander Hassenstein – UEFA/UEFA via Getty He told viewers in confessional footage that he “didn’t think at the beginning that [the relationship] would be this strong, that I would fall in love with her. I didn’t expect it, honestly. But after a while, I felt that she was the woman of my life.” Reflecting on Ronaldo’s surprise marriage proposal in a December 2025 interview with Elle Spain , Rodríguez shared that she was “shocked” in the moment. “The truth is, when he proposed, it was the last thing on my mind,” she told the magazine. “It took me a long time to process the enormous stone he gave me. I was so shocked that I left it in my room and didn’t open it in the sunlight until the next day.” As for her jaw-dropping ring, she declared it “gorgeous,” before joking, “It’s the least he could offer me after 10 years of waiting.”

items.title: Political parties, judiciary must reform themselves to protect Africa’s democracy – Asiedu Nketia
items.description: National Chairman of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Johnson Asiedu Nketia, has called for fundamental reforms within political parties and the judiciary, arguing that the two institutions cannot protect African democracy if they lack credibility, accountability and public trust. According to him, political parties must move beyond functioning as electoral machines and become permanent democratic institutions, while the judiciary must remain independent and provide justice that is accessible, impartial, timely and credible. Mr Asiedu Nketia made the call on Tuesday, August 11, 2026, when he participated in the 2026 Goodluck Jonathan Foundation Democracy Dialogue in Bauchi, Nigeria. The dialogue was held on the theme: “Beyond Elections: Can Political Parties and the Judiciary Save African Democracy?” Speaking on the panel on political parties and the judiciary and the need to rebuild trust in democratic institutions, Mr Asiedu Nketia said neither political parties nor the courts could save democracy merely by existing. “Political parties cannot save democracy when they function only as electoral machines, instruments of patronage or vehicles for individual ambition,” he said. “Courts cannot save democracy when they are inaccessible, slow, inconsistent or perceived to be subject to political influence. Both institutions can defend democracy only when they are themselves credible, accountable, competent and trusted.” Democracy goes beyond elections Mr Asiedu Nketia said elections only determine who receives the authority to govern and do not, on their own, guarantee that political power will subsequently be exercised lawfully. He said democracy must also be measured by whether constitutional limits are respected, opposition parties are allowed to operate legitimately and governments remain accountable to citizens between elections. “Elections determine who receives the authority to govern. They do not, by themselves, determine whether that authority will be exercised lawfully, whether constitutional limits will be respected, whether the opposition will remain legitimate or whether government will improve the lives of the people,” he said. “Democracy is therefore tested not only on election day, but in every decision taken between one election and the next.” Ghana’s democratic record Mr Asiedu Nketia cited Ghana’s Fourth Republic as an example of democratic institutionalisation, although he cautioned against complacency. He noted that Ghana had held nine consecutive general elections since 1992, with four elections—in 2000, 2008, 2016 and 2024—resulting in the transfer of power from one political party to another. He said the peaceful alternation of power demonstrated that an African governing party could lose an election, hand over power peacefully and subsequently return to government through the ballot box rather than force. He cited the 2008 presidential election as a particularly important example. Professor John Evans Atta Mills won the election with 50.23 per cent of the vote against 49.77 per cent for Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo, a margin of less than one percentage point. Mr Asiedu Nketia said the ability of political leaders, state institutions and citizens to prevent such a close contest from becoming a national crisis was itself an important democratic achievement. He also cited the 2016 election, when then-President John Dramani Mahama conceded defeat and oversaw the transition of power, and the 2024 election, when then-Vice-President Mahamudu Bawumia conceded before the formal declaration after his party’s collation indicated that the result could not be overturned. “These concessions were not ceremonial courtesies; they were constitutional contributions,” he said. However, Mr Asiedu Nketia warned that Ghana’s democratic record should not lead to complacency. He pointed to the 2020 election, which resulted in a Parliament comprising 137 members from each of the two major parties and one independent member, but was also marked by election-related violence in which eight people were reportedly killed. “This reminds us that democratic progress is never irreversible,” he said. Political parties must reform Mr Asiedu Nketia said political parties had responsibilities beyond winning elections and should not be treated as the private property of founders, financiers, office holders or temporary leaders. He said parties perform important public and constitutional functions, including recruiting political leaders, developing policy alternatives, organising political participation and connecting citizens to the state. “A party that demands credible national elections must conduct credible internal elections. A party that condemns authoritarianism in government must tolerate legitimate disagreement within its own structures,” he said. He also called for greater inclusion of women, young people and persons with disabilities in political leadership. Mr Asiedu Nketia said the growing cost of political participation posed a serious threat to internal party democracy because it could make wealth rather than competence the principal requirement for seeking political office. He cited research by the Westminster Foundation for Democracy and CDD-Ghana which found that the cost of contesting parliamentary office increased by 59 per cent between the 2012 and 2016 electoral cycles, reaching an average of GH¢389,803. He further cited a CDD-Ghana study which estimated that a viable parliamentary campaign by 2020, including the cost of maintaining a constituency presence, could require about GH¢4 million. “When entry into political leadership becomes this expensive, parties risk selecting the wealthiest rather than the most capable, while elected officials may enter office burdened by financiers and expectations of repayment,” he said. Parties need policy and leadership institutions Mr Asiedu Nketia said political parties should also reclaim their policy development, civic education and leadership training functions. He proposed permanent research institutions within political parties to develop policies, train candidates and office holders and assess governments formed under their platforms. “Democracy suffers when public office becomes the first place at which political leaders begin to learn the responsibilities of government,” he said. He also called for measurable progress on the participation of women and young people in political leadership. He noted that women occupied only 40 of Ghana’s 276 parliamentary seats, representing 14.5 per cent, despite making up slightly more than half of the country’s population. He said young people between 15 and 35 constituted 38.2 per cent of Ghana’s population, yet no member of the current Parliament was aged 30 or younger at the beginning of the legislature. Political parties, he argued, must create pathways that allow women and young people to move beyond campaign mobilisation into policy development, party leadership, Parliament and executive responsibility. Judiciary must win public confidence Turning to the judiciary, Mr Asiedu Nketia said courts remained indispensable to democracy because political competition inevitably produced disputes involving elections, fundamental rights and constitutional boundaries. He cited Ghana’s presidential election petitions following the 2012 and 2020 elections as examples of how major political disagreements could be transferred from the streets to the courtroom. The 2012 petition was dismissed by a five-to-four majority after an extended hearing, while the 2020 petition was unanimously dismissed by the Supreme Court. According to Mr Asiedu Nketia, political actors complied with both decisions despite disagreements over aspects of the proceedings and the reasoning of the court. He said respect for judicial authority, however, did not require political actors to surrender their right to criticise judicial reasoning. “Legitimate criticism is part of constitutional democracy; intimidation, threats and personal attacks are not,” he said. He added that judicial independence should not be interpreted as freedom from ethical standards, transparency, consistency or public accountability. Concerns over access to justice Mr Asiedu Nketia said public confidence in the judiciary was an issue that could not be ignored. Citing Afrobarometer’s Round 10 findings, he said only 35 per cent of Ghanaians trusted the courts “somewhat” or “a lot”. He said half of respondents were not confident that an ordinary person who had been wronged could obtain justice, while only 37 per cent believed they could afford to take a legal problem to court. Only 38 per cent believed that a case would be resolved within a reasonable period, he added. Mr Asiedu Nketia stressed that the figures represented public perceptions rather than judicial findings but said such perceptions had implications for institutional legitimacy. “Judicial authority cannot depend only on constitutional text; it must also rest on citizens’ confidence that justice is accessible, impartial and timely,” he said. Courts must exercise restraint Mr Asiedu Nketia called for a judiciary that was strong enough to restrain governments, protect opposition parties, defend fundamental rights and enforce constitutional limits. At the same time, he cautioned courts against becoming “alternative political chambers” or replacing decisions properly entrusted to elected institutions and citizens. He said judicial courage must therefore be accompanied by restraint. Proposed reforms Mr Asiedu Nketia proposed a number of reforms aimed at strengthening democratic institutions. For political parties, he called for enforceable standards on internal democracy, campaign financing, audited accounts, candidate selection and leadership succession. He also called for the publication of measurable data on women’s and youth participation, measures to reduce the financial barriers to political candidature and the establishment of permanent policy and leadership institutions. On the judiciary, he advocated transparent criteria for judicial appointments and promotions, the prompt publication of constitutional judgments, stronger legal aid services and the publication of reliable information on court performance. He also called for political parties, courts, electoral bodies, civil society organisations, the media and academic institutions to engage in dialogue before political crises emerge. “Dialogue should not begin only when an election dispute threatens national stability,” he said. ‘Parties and judiciary must reform themselves’ In his concluding remarks, Mr Asiedu Nketia said political parties and the judiciary could contribute significantly to safeguarding democracy in Africa, but only if they were willing to reform themselves. “Political parties must cease to be seasonal electoral machines and become permanent democratic institutions,” he said. “The judiciary must remain independent of political power while providing remedies that are impartial, accessible, timely and convincingly reasoned.” He argued that the future of African democracy would not be secured merely by conducting more elections but by building institutions that make elections meaningful, governments accountable, constitutional limits effective and peaceful transfers of power normal. “Political parties must remember that power is temporary and that the state belongs to the people,” he said. “The judiciary must understand that its strongest protection is not the goodwill of political leaders, but the confidence of citizens in its independence and integrity.” Mr Asiedu Nketia said democracy would become durable when political parties respected constitutional limits, courts administered justice without fear or favour, governments delivered tangible improvements in people’s lives and citizens remained engaged beyond election day. “Democracy becomes more than a procedure. It becomes a durable system of public trust, peaceful competition, accountable authority and national development,” he said.

items.title: Félix Tshisekedi lance les travaux du boulevard Docteur Étienne Tshisekedi wa Mulumba à Kinshasa
items.description: Le président de la République, Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi Tshilombo, a officiellement lancé, mardi 11 août 2026, les travaux de construction du boulevard Docteur Étienne Tshisekedi wa Mulumba à Kinshasa. Ce projet d’infrastructure, porté par le gouvernement provincial, vise à améliorer durablement la mobilité urbaine dans la capitale congolaise, confrontée à une circulation de plus en plus dense.

items.title: Tougan : « Vous prenez soin des populations. A notre tour de prendre soin de vous », dixit le ministre aux agents de santé
items.description: Le Camarade ministre de la Santé, Dr Robert Lucien Jean-Claude Kargougou, a effectué, ce lundi 10 août 2026, une visite de terrain au Centre médical avec antenne chirurgicale (CMA) et au district sanitaire de Tougan, dans la région du Sourou. Une visite placée sous le signe de l’écoute et de la proximité avec les professionnels de santé. Le camarade ministre était accompagné du gouverneur des régions du bankuy et du sourou. Avant d’échanger avec les agents, le ministre a parcouru les différents services du CMA et du district sanitaire. De service en service, il s’est intéressé aux conditions de travail des équipes, au fonctionnement des unités et aux réalités auxquelles elles sont confrontées au quotidien. Cette immersion lui a permis de toucher du doigt les difficultés vécues par les professionnels qui assurent la continuité des soins dans un contexte particulièrement exigeant. La visite s’est poursuivie par une rencontre avec les agents, en présence des autorités administratives de la province et des régions. Les échanges ont porté sur plusieurs préoccupations, notamment les ressources humaines, les infrastructures, les équipements, la logistique et les contraintes liées à la situation sécuritaire. Présentant la situation du district, le médecin-chef, Dr Jérôme Nikièma, a également mis en lumière les efforts consentis par les équipes et les acteurs communautaires pour maintenir les services essentiels. Selon les données présentées, les agents de santé à base communautaire ont notamment contribué à la réalisation de plus de 1 600 accouchements au cours d’un semestre, illustrant leur rôle dans la continuité des soins. Pour le ministre de la Santé, cette démarche répond à une orientation claire : aller sur le terrain pour mieux comprendre les réalités et apporter des réponses adaptées. « C’est pour cela qu’aujourd’hui, je suis venu à Tougan pour voir, pour écouter, pour comprendre afin de mieux agir », a-t-il déclaré. Dr Robert Kargougou a salué le courage, le patriotisme et la résilience des agents qui continuent d’assurer leurs missions malgré les contraintes liées à l’insécurité. Il a également exprimé sa solidarité aux professionnels ayant vécu des situations traumatisantes et insisté sur l’importance de la prise en compte de leur santé mentale. Un hommage a par ailleurs été rendu aux agents de santé tombés dans l’exercice de leur mission. Face à la vétusté de certains bâtiments du CMA, le ministre a évoqué les perspectives d’amélioration des infrastructures, notamment à travers leur réhabilitation ou leur remplacement, afin d’offrir de meilleures conditions de travail aux agents et de prise en charge aux patients. Une visite vécue comme un encouragement Pour les agents, la présence du premier responsable du département, qui a pris le temps de visiter leurs services puis d’écouter directement leurs préoccupations, constitue un signal fort de considération et un véritable encouragement à poursuivre leurs efforts malgré les difficultés. En clôturant les échanges, le ministre a réaffirmé l’attention portée aux préoccupations exprimées et la volonté du ministère de poursuivre les efforts pour améliorer les conditions de travail et la qualité des soins. « Vous prenez soin des populations. À notre tour de prendre soin de vous. » À Tougan, cette visite aura ainsi permis au ministre de mieux appréhender les réalités du terrain, mais aussi aux agents de se sentir écoutés, reconnus et encouragés à poursuivre leur engagement au service des populations. Avant le début de sa visite de terrain, le Camarade ministre de la Santé a présenté ses civilités au chef de Tougan, en signe de considération à l’égard de l’autorité coutumière. DCRP/MS

items.title: Sebta : Il est temps d’éduquer à l’information
items.description: « L’erreur ne se propage, ne s’amplifie, ne vit enfin qu’à une condition : trouver dans la société où elle se répand un bouillon de culture favorable ». On peut aisément appliquer cette réflexion du célèbre historien Marc Bloch (1886-1944), formulée dans son essai sur les « fausses nouvelles de la guerre » (1921), au cas des événements dramatiques Sebta. Pour le spécialiste du Moyen Âge et cofondateur de l’École des Annales, dont l’entrée au Panthéon a été annoncée en juin 2026, « une fausse nouvelle naît toujours de représentations collectives qui préexistent à sa naissance ; elle n’est fortuite qu’en apparence ou, plus précisément, tout ce qu’il y a de fortuit en elle, c’est l’incident initial, absolument quelconque, qui déclenche le travail des imaginations ; mais cette mise en branle n’a lieu que parce que les imaginations sont déjà préparées et fermentent sourdement ». L’événement de la ruée migratoire spectaculaire vers l’enclave montre à quel point de faux récits peuvent soulever des foules et provoquer des comportements aux conséquences tragiques. Près d’un siècle après la publication de ses réflexions, Marc Bloch éclaire avec une étonnante acuité cette triste actualité. Va-t-on attendre une nouvelle déflagration ? Va-t-on attendre l’explosion d’une autre bombe aux éclats ravageurs et aux nombreuses victimes collatérales, à l’image de celle de Sebta, avant de prendre à bras-le-corps la question de l’éducation à l’information ? Des Marocains sont morts. D’autres ont risqué leur vie après avoir cru à des publications, devenues virales sur les réseaux sociaux, selon lesquelles les portes de l’Espagne leur étaient grandes ouvertes. Il aurait suffi de traverser la frontière à la nage et le tour était joué ! Bien évidemment, la désinformation, menée à grande échelle, dans l’espace numérique, n’explique pas à elle seule cette tragique ruée migratoire. Elle en a été l’élément de déflagration , la première étincelle d’une action collective massive dont les causes sont autrement plus profondes. La désinformation se nourrit du désespoir et peut le transformer en mouvement collectif. Une responsabilité publique Aussi dramatiques soient-ils, les événements de Sebta peuvent contribuer à une véritable prise de conscience collective. Aux réponses institutionnelles de nature sécuritaire, politique, sociale et économique attendues et apportées dans le cadre de la gestion de cette crise, il y a lieu d’intégrer une dimension clé, à savoir l’éducation à l’information . Elle relève d’un intérêt vital. Une responsabilité envers les citoyens et, dans certaines circonstances, une véritable question de sécurité nationale. Si on prend le cas des jeunes par exemple, ils ne se tournent plus vers les médias classiques pour s’informer. Les réseaux sociaux, les plateformes numériques et désormais les outils d’intelligence artificielle occupent une place centrale dans leur rapport à l’information. Il y a donc une grande bataille à mener. Pas celle qui consisterait à détourner les jeunes des internets, encore moins à leur en interdire l’accès jusqu’à un certain âge. La véritable bataille consiste à investir massivement dans l’éducation à l’information . Apprendre au jeune public à vérifier une source, à identifier une fake news, à distinguer un fait d’une opinion, à repérer une tentative de manipulation, à contextualiser une image ou une vidéo et à comprendre les mécanismes de viralité. Ne pas confondre ce qui est viral avec ce qui est vrai . Tout un combat. Un tel chantier nécessite une véritable volonté politique, une stratégie nationale et un investissement durable dans l’école, la formation, la société civile et les médias. Sebta, un cas d’école Dans ce domaine, le drame de Sebta représente un sérieux cas d’étude. Entre les publications qui ont circulé sur les réseaux sociaux et les traitements médiatiques, différents selon qu’ils provenaient de médias espagnols ou marocains, il existe une matière éditoriale particulièrement riche à décoder et en tirer des enseigneents : Comment une information est-elle née ? Qui l’a diffusée ? Pourquoi est-elle devenue virale ? Comment a-t-elle été reprise ? Quels mots ont été employés ? Quelles images ont accompagné les récits ? Qu’est-ce qui relève du fait, de l’interprétation, de l’analyse et de l’opinion ? Autant de questions qui devraient devenir des réflexes. Il s’agit, en définitive, de développer une véritable culture de la consommation de l’information , fondée sur une méthode et sur un esprit critique à l’égard des supports médiatiques et communicationnels, dans leur acception la plus large. Il ne s’agit évidemment pas de distribuer des notes ni de désigner les «bons» et les «mauvais» médias. Le questionnement doit être le fil conducteur de toute consommation médiatique, sans pour autant tomber dans le piège du doute permanent et de la remise en cause systématique de tout ce qui est publié. Au final, l’intérêt est de se forger une opinion solide en distinguant le vrai du faux, le fait de l’opinion, l’information de la manipulation. Pouvoirs publics, société civile et médias En matière d’éducation à l’information, les pouvoirs publics doivent donner l’exemple. Lorsqu’un gouvernement reste silencieux sur des sujets ou des affaires d’une importance capitale pour les citoyens, il peut contribuer à alimenter le doute et l’inquiétude. Le silence institutionnel peut être dévastateur lorsqu’il laisse le champ libre aux rumeurs et à la désinformation, qui peuvent alors se propager et finir par convaincre les esprits les plus vulnérables. La responsabilité des partis politiques est également cruciale. L’encadrement partisan doit prendre en charge cette question de manière sérieuse et professionnelle. La société civile, elle aussi, est appelée à jouer un rôle majeur de sensibilisation, d’accompagnement et d’encadrement. Et les médias ? Il est difficile de demander aux citoyens d’exercer leur esprit critique face à l’information lorsque le paysage médiatique lui-même est fragile. On ne peut pas construire une société résiliente face à la désinformation avec des médias affaiblis. Seule une politique volontariste et durable d’éducation à l’information et la présence de médias professionnels, indépendants et forts, sont en mesure développer la capacité des citoyens à distinguer l’information de la manipulation. Et parfois, cette capacité peut tout simplement sauver des vies. The post Sebta : Il est temps d’éduquer à l’information appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Koulsé/Souveraineté énergétique : une centrale thermique de 25 MW inaugurée à Kaya
items.description: Koulsé/Souveraineté énergétique : une centrale thermique de 25 MW inaugurée à Kaya Kaya, 11 août 2026 (AIB)-Le ministre de l'Énergie, des Mines et des Carrières, Yacouba Zabré Gouba, a déclaré mardi que la centrale thermique de Kaya, d'une puissance de 25 MW, constitue un pas supplémentaire du Burkina Faso vers la souveraineté énergétique et le renforcement de sa capacité nationale de production d'électricité. « Il n'y a pas d'industrialisation durable sans énergie disponible. Il n'y a pas de transformation de nos productions sans énergie fiable », a affirmé le ministre lors de l'inauguration officielle de l'infrastructure. La cérémonie d'inauguration s'est déroulée en présence notamment du ministre de l'Enseignement secondaire, professionnel et technique, Moumouni Zoungrana, de la ministre déléguée chargée de la Coopération régionale, Bêbgnasgnan Stella Eldine Kabré/Kaboré, du ministre délégué chargé des Ressources animales, Dr Amadou Dicko, du ministre de la Construction de la Patrie, Mikaïlou Sidibé, ainsi que des autorités administratives et locales, conduites par la gouverneure par intérim de la région des Koulsé, Bernadette Adenyo/Sermé. Réalisée dans le cadre d'un partenariat public-privé (PPP) avec BUTEC comme partenaire, la centrale a nécessité un investissement de 23,47 millions d'euros, soit environ 15,4 milliards de FCFA. Elle est équipée de 28 moteurs Cummins d'une puissance unitaire de 1 000 kW, fonctionnant au diesel, pour une puissance installée de 25 MW. Pour Yacouba Zabré Gouba, cette infrastructure traduit la volonté des autorités burkinabè de renforcer les capacités nationales de production d'électricité, tout en réduisant progressivement la dépendance énergétique du pays. « Le Burkina Faso refuse la fatalité » et entend « produire davantage et dépendre moins », a-t-il soutenu. La centrale thermique de Kaya est, selon lui, la quatrième réalisée en 2026 après celles de Koudougou, Bobo-Dioulasso et Pabré, portant à plus de 126 MW les nouvelles productions nationales. « Le Burkina Faso prévoit également la réalisation de trois autres centrales, notamment à Komsilga, d'une puissance de 50 MW, à Donsin, pour 27 MW, et à Zagtouli, pour 17 MW », a-t-il promis. L'administrateur général de BUTEC, Sleima Abi Ghanem, s'est réjoui de la réalisation de la centrale, estimant qu'elle représente « bien plus qu'un ouvrage énergétique ». La présidente de la Délégation spéciale communale de Kaya, Solange Kima/Minoungou, a souligné l'importance de l'électricité pour les entreprises, les commerces, les administrations, les établissements scolaires et les centres de santé de sa commune. « Sans énergie fiable, il ne peut y avoir de transformation économique durable », a-t-elle déclaré. Pour la responsable communale, la nouvelle infrastructure contribuera à répondre aux besoins croissants des populations et des activités économiques, tout en ouvrant de nouvelles perspectives pour l'investissement, l'entrepreneuriat et l’emploi des jeunes. Agence d'information du Burkina AIO/ata

items.title: Supercoupe d’Europe 2026 : le PSG favori face à Aston Villa, ce mercredi 12 août
items.description: La Supercoupe d’Europe, une compétition opposant le vainqueur de la Ligue des Champions au vainqueur de la Ligue Europa de la saison sportive écoulée, se jouera ce mercredi 12 août 2026 à Salzbourg (Autriche). Elle opposera le Paris Saint-Germain, double champion d’Europe aux Anglais d’Aston Villa, vainqueurs de la Ligue Europa. De l’avis de tous les observateurs et analystes sportifs avertis, les Parisiens partent largement avec la faveur des pronostics pour s’offrir un deuxième titre dans cette compétition. L’année dernière, l’on s’en souvient, ils ont remporté leur premier titre en Supercoupe d’Europe aux dépens d’un autre club anglais (Tottenham). Mais comme le football se promène souvent avec son cortège de surprises, les poulains de Luis Enrique auront grand intérêt à ne pas prendre de haut leurs adversaires du jour. La saison dernière, la formation d’Aston Villa a montré de bonnes choses en Premier League et sur la scène européenne. Le club phare de Birmingham a remporté, 44 ans après son sacre en C1 (actuelle Ligue des Champions de l’UEFA), son deuxième trophée dans les compétitions européennes de football. Une victoire historique à mettre évidemment à l’actif de son entraîneur espagnol Unai Emery, qui totalise désormais 5 titres en Ligue Europa (3 avec le FC Séville, 1 avec Villarreal et 1 avec Aston Villa). A noter que le Real Madrid, avec ses 6 titres, est le club le plus capé en Supercoupe d’Europe. Le club madrilène est suivi de son grand rival, le FC Barcelone (5 titres), de l’AC Milan (5 titres), de Liverpool FC (4 titres) et de l’Atlético de Madrid (3 titres). Les clubs ayant remporté deux fois la compétition sont : Bayern Munich, Chelsea, Juventus, Anderlecht, Valence, Ajax Amsterdam. Le Paris Saint-Germain va-t-il rejoindre ce club des doubles vainqueurs de la Supercoupe d’Europe ? Attendons de voir. Almamy Samadou L’article Supercoupe d’Europe 2026 : le PSG favori face à Aston Villa, ce mercredi 12 août est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Algérie – Maroc : le président du Sénat accuse le Makhzen « d’ambitions expansionnistes »
items.description: Le président du Conseil de la nation (Sénat) Azouz Nasri a salué ce mardi la résistance du peuple sahraoui contre l’occupant marocain, réitéré la position de l’Algérie sur le conflit au Sahara occidental et fustigé les « ambitions expansionnistes » du Makhzen dans la région. L’occasion pour lui d'adresser quelques messages sur la position de l’Algérie concernant ce conflit. La RASD organise son Université d’été en Algérie en présence de Brahim Ghali Nasri s’exprimait dans un message adressé à la 14ᵉédition de l’Université d’été des cadres de la République arabe sahraouie démocratique et du Front Polisario, qui se déroule à Boumerdès. Cette rencontre est présidée par Brahim Ghali, président de la RASD. Le président du Sénat algérien a salué la « résistance, le courage et la constance, dont fait preuve le peuple sahraoui dans son choix, ainsi que son attachement à ses revendications sous la conduite de son seul représentant légitime, le Front Polisario ». Cette résistance, a-t-il dit, « mérite la considération du monde et exige une vaste mobilisation solidaire internationale, à même de barrer la voie au projet de colonisation de peuplement du Makhzen marocain dans la région et de mettre un terme à ses ambitions expansionnistes fondées sur des prétentions illusoires, rejetées par les témoignages de l’Histoire et catégoriquement réfutées par la Cour internationale de Justice dans sa décision historique et équitable. » Il a exprimé la « fierté » de l’Algérie de se « tenir aux côtés du peuple sahraoui résistant dans son combat existentiel ». Sahara occidental : l’Algérie refuse la perpétuation du conflit Le président du Conseil de la nation a souligné que l’Algérie se trouve à « l’avant-garde du soutien diplomatique international croissant visant à imposer un règlement juste que le peuple sahraoui accepte librement et conformément à sa volonté ». L’Algérie, a-t-il dit, refuse la « perpétuation du conflit à travers la prorogation de mesures provisoires et la tentative d’imposer des solutions infondées, contournant la légalité internationale et reconfigurant le colonialisme sous une nouvelle forme de domination. » Azouz Nasri a souligné que « l’élimination du colonialisme » en Palestine et au Sahara occidental constitue un « devoir » et une « responsabilité collectifs », et que le droit à l’autodétermination est un « droit imprescriptible et inaliénable. » Il a mis en garde contre l’impact sur la paix et la sécurité internationales de « l’affaiblissement de ce droit par la complaisance à l’égard de l’État occupant ». L’article Algérie – Maroc : le président du Sénat accuse le Makhzen « d'ambitions expansionnistes » est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Santé mentale : Un plan stratégique pour lutter contre le burn-out (3/5)
items.description: Au Sénégal, la santé mentale en milieu professionnel est devenue une préoccupation majeure. L’enquête nationale sur la santé mentale réalisée en 2023 a révélé une prévalence du burn-out de 57,5 % chez les travailleurs, mettant en lumière l’ampleur de l’épuisement professionnel dans le pays. Face à cette situation, le Plan stratégique de santé mentale 2024-2028 intègre désormais la question du bien-être psychologique au travail à travers plusieurs axes d’intervention, allant de la gouvernance à la réinsertion socioprofessionnelle des personnes atteintes de troubles mentaux. Dans ce cadre, la Division de la santé mentale (DSM) s’est dotée d’un bureau dédié à la santé mentale en milieu scolaire et professionnel. Cette structure a pour mission de promouvoir le bien-être psychologique, mais aussi de prévenir et de prendre en charge les troubles mentaux dans les environnements de travail et d’apprentissage. Le document stratégique met également en évidence plusieurs défis liés au monde professionnel. Parmi eux figurent le stress professionnel, présenté comme une conséquence de la précarité économique et des fortes charges de dépendance pesant sur les travailleurs, avec des répercussions sur leur rendement. Le personnel de santé est particulièrement exposé au risque de burn-out, alors que le suivi psychologique reste insuffisant. Le manque de sensibilisation au sein des entreprises constitue aussi un obstacle important, tout comme la stigmatisation et l’exclusion dont peuvent être victimes les personnes souffrant de troubles mentaux dans les espaces professionnels. Le plan accorde par ailleurs une place importante à la réinsertion socioprofessionnelle. Les autorités ambitionnent d’atteindre un taux de 50 % de réinsertion des personnes vivant avec des troubles mentaux ou des handicaps psychosociaux. L’objectif spécifique n° 6 prévoit notamment un accompagnement vers l’autonomie sociale et professionnelle. La création de centres médico-éducatifs est également envisagée afin de préparer les personnes concernées à une meilleure intégration dans le monde du travail. Entre 2024 et 2028, plusieurs actions sont programmées pour améliorer la prise en charge de la santé mentale en milieu professionnel. Il est notamment prévu d’organiser des rencontres de plaidoyer avec différents ministères, dont celui de l’Entrepreneuriat, afin d’intégrer davantage les questions de santé mentale dans les politiques publiques. Des campagnes de sensibilisation seront aussi menées pour favoriser la réinsertion professionnelle des personnes souffrant de troubles mentaux et lutter contre les préjugés au sein des entreprises. Enfin, des mécanismes de suivi et d’évaluation permettront de mesurer les progrès réalisés en matière d’insertion professionnelle des personnes concernées. Arame NDIAYE Lire aussi : Pr Abou Sy, psychiatre : « Dès l’instant où le travail devient une source de souffrance, on peut parler de burn-out » (2/5)

items.title: Luv FM High School Debate: T.I AMASS advances as IBASS makes impressive debut
items.description: T.I. Ahmadiyya Senior High School–Kumasi and Ibadur Rahman Academy have advanced to the next round of the 2026 LUV FM Kel-Charcoal High School Debate after impressive victories on Day Two of the competition. The second day of the competition, held at the Christian Service University, delivered two engaging contests as students showcased their knowledge, critical thinking, confidence and ability to defend their positions under pressure. The two schools emerged victorious after hard-fought battles against Okomfo Anokye SHS and Mankranso SHS, respectively. The battle of intellects and fearless debaters continued with two action-packed contests, as emotion met logic in very powerful deliveries. The opening contest of the day saw Mankranso SHS take on Ibadur Rahman Academy on the motion: “ECG should be privatized.” Mankranso SHS argued in favor of the motion, while Ibadur Rahman Academy opposed it. Both sides presented well-structured arguments and backed their positions with facts and logical reasoning. The contest also featured spirited rebuttals, making it a closely watched encounter. At the end of the contest, however, Ibadur Rahman Academy emerged victorious with 210 points against Mankranso SHS’s 185, winning by a majority decision of the judges. The victory sent the Ibadur Rahman camp into celebration, with the school’s Patron, Mr. Sabato, expressing confidence in the team’s ability to compete against any opponent in the subsequent stages. “Today, we have announced to the whole of Ghana that indeed IBASS is here, and we are ready for anyone that comes our way,” he said. The second contest produced another intriguing battle, with T.I. Amass, Kumasi facing Okomfo Anokye SHS, debating the motion: “MMDCEs should be elected.” T.I. Amass argued for the motion, while Okomfo Anokye took the opposing position. The two schools delivered strong arguments and counterarguments, with the rebuttal stage providing some of the most intense moments of the contest. T.I. Amass, however, eventually established its dominance and secured a 213–192 victory, defeating Okomfo Anokye by a 21-point margin through a unanimous decision of the judges. The victory will come as a boost to the inaugural champions, who are once again setting their sights on the ultimate prize as they would tell us they are coming for what they believe is truly theirs. The principal speaker for T.I. Amass made the team’s intentions clear after their victory. “We are ready for whoever comes our way. We are AMASS, and we are not going down without a fight.” With the conclusion of Day Two, Ibadur Rahman Academy and T.I. Amass SHS join Kumasi Wesley Girls SHS and Christian Service Senior High School (CHRISSEC) as the first four schools to book their places in the next round. The competition is expected to intensify as more schools take to the stage to battle for qualification and ultimately the championship. The 2026 edition of the LUV FM Kel-Charcoal High School Debate continues to provide a platform for students to demonstrate their intellectual ability, public speaking skills and confidence while engaging with topical issues of national interest. SIM Group of Companies emerged as a standout recipient, earning acclaim for its comprehensive and forward-thinking approach to integrated business solutions. The Most Outstanding in Integrated Business Solutions award reflects SIM Group’s ability to seamlessly combine multiple service offerings into cohesive, efficient, and client-focused solutions. The company has consistently demonstrated expertise in delivering tailored services that meet the evolving needs of businesses, positioning itself as a reliable partner across diverse industries. This recognition highlights the company’s strategic focus on innovation, operational efficiency, and value-driven service delivery. By integrating technology, management systems, and customer-centric approaches, SIM Group has successfully created solutions that enhance productivity and support business growth. Over the years, SIM Group of Companies has built a strong reputation grounded in professionalism, consistency, and a clear vision for sustainable growth. items.title: What Do Sex and Gender Even Mean Now?
items.description: In her first argument as a lawyer before the Supreme Court, Ruth Bader Ginsburg famously quoted the abolitionist Sarah Grimké, who said, “I ask no favor for my sex. All I ask of our brethren is that they take their feet off our necks.” At some point, however, Ginsburg was encouraged to use an alternative to the term sex . “I’m typing all these briefs and articles for you and the word sex, sex, sex is on every page,” her secretary at Columbia Law School told her. “Don’t you know that those nine men”—that era’s Supreme Court justices—“they hear that word, and their first association is not the way you want them to be thinking?” The secretary suggested substituting gender to “ward off distracting associations.” But sex and gender don’t mean the same thing. The two terms have never been stable. Still, I recall a time when, among educated people, sex was typically understood to refer to matters of biology, such as a person’s reproductive organs, and gender to refer to matters that are socially constructed, such as the norm of dressing little boys in blue pants and little girls in pink dresses. Today, there seems to be no standard usage. Parents throw gender-reveal parties to disclose the sex of their baby. President Trump said in his 2025 inaugural address, “It will henceforth be the official policy of the United States government that there are only two genders: male and female”—but “male” and “female” are sexes. A statute in California defines sex (in part) as follows: “‘Sex’ also includes, but is not limited to, a person’s gender. ‘Gender’ means sex, and includes a person’s gender identity and gender expression.” The confusion that results from this lost distinction causes problems in academia––see the recent kerfuffle in anthropology ––as well as in medicine, law, public policy, and more. People mistake meanings and talk past one another about matters that are fraught even when definitions are clear. How did we get into this semantic mess? The concept of a “gender role” was introduced in a 1955 paper by the researcher John Money to signify “all those things that a person says or does to disclose himself or herself as having the status of boy or man, girl or woman.” He believed that people born with ambiguous or atypical genitals, whom he called “hermaphrodites or intersexes,” contributed to “this new meaning of gender.” Would such individuals operate in society as men or women? He thought that rearing would better predict a person’s “gender role” than biology. The term gender identity , first defined as “one’s sense of being a member of a particular sex,” dates back to at least the early 1960s. The psychoanalyst Robert Stoller wrote that “gender role is the overt behavior one displays in society, the role which he plays.” By the ’70s, feminists were the most prominent group to adopt gender and related terms, using them to differentiate biological differences between men and women from differences imposed by society. In the 1972 book Sex, Gender, and Society , the feminist sociologist Ann Oakley suggested that biology may play little or no role in determining gender identity (that is, one’s sense of being a member of a particular sex). If a biological predisposition to a male or female gender identity exists at all, she wrote, it “may be decisively and ineradicably overridden by cultural learning.” In the 1990 book Gender Trouble , Judith Butler challenged the common assumption that gender mirrors sex and is binary, arguing that “a gender cannot be said to follow from a sex in any one way.” Butler also argued that “perhaps this construct called ‘sex’ is as culturally constructed as gender,” and the supposed distinction between them “turns out to be no distinction at all.” In 1997, the sex researcher Milton Diamond and the psychiatrist Keith Sigmundson reached the conclusion that sex is a distinct and important category. The two revisited a case that Money had included in his research. “The penis of an XY individual was accidentally ablated”—that is to say, severely damaged or removed—“and he was subsequently raised as a female,” the authors recounted. “Initially this individual was described as developing into a normally functioning female.” Money had treated the case as confirmation that nurture reliably overrides nature. But the story later changed: When older, the patient rejected “this sex of rearing” and “switched at puberty to living as a male.” This mattered in part because, the authors explained, “the standard in instances of extensive penile damage to infants is to recommend rearing the male as a female.” They urged doctors to reconsider that practice. The importance of sex as a category was further affirmed in 2001 by a group of experts convened by the Institute of Medicine (since renamed the National Academy of Medicine). Recounting several public-health guidelines that excluded women of child-bearing age from clinical trials on the erroneous assumption that they “will not differ significantly in response to treatment in most situations,” the report noted: “Sex, that is, being male or female,” is “an important basic human variable that should be considered when designing, analyzing, and reporting findings from studies.” But the importance of sex as a category of study did not guarantee sex a stable place in scholarship, as the Harvard evolutionary biologist David Haig showed by documenting a dramatic decline in the term sex and a rise in gender in the titles of academic articles between 1945 and 2001. At first, feminist scholarship converged on socially constructed gender and biologically determined sex , Haig wrote, but “that distinction was difficult to maintain,” because “no term remained to refer to situations in which causation was unknown, disputed, or involved an interaction between biology and culture.” Soon gender spread to other disciplines, and eventually gender rather than sex began to appear even in scholarship on the physiology of animals. “Among the reasons that working scientists have given me for choosing gender rather than sex in biological contexts,” Haig wrote, “are desires to signal sympathy with feminist goals, to use a more academic term, or to avoid the connotation of copulation.” By the 2000s, yet another obstacle to mutual understanding arose: What people meant by gender was changing, not only in academic discourse, but in popular usage . For many of the early feminists, gender was a cage built by society. Parents gave little girls but not little boys Easy-Bake Ovens, reproducing a gendered expectation that girls would grow up to do the cooking. But as the decades wore on, gender came to carry a second meaning, one very different from social norms imposed from the outside. The term now sometimes refers to an internal aspect of a person’s sense of self, or even the essence of who they truly are. While some people kept using gender as shorthand for something from which they sought liberation––to weaken gender norms was to fight the patriarchy––others saw it as an identity, perhaps innate, that individuals discerned and expressed, and that a just society ought to affirm. In 2014, Facebook announced that users would no longer have to identify as male or female––they could choose among at least 58 “gender” options (including intersex , a term that tells us something about a person’s reproductive or sexual anatomy but not about their gender identity). That brings us to the present era, when sex and gender loom larger than ever in political, legal, and cultural debates––but usage keeps changing faster than the public can keep up, and many semantic choices are made for reasons other than advancing shared understanding. Three examples help illustrate the dysfunction that can result: When Australia asked individuals to note their sex in its 2021 census, the form gave three options: male, female, and nonbinary, “to allow respondents to participate in the Census when the male and female sex categories did not accurately describe their sex,” the Australian Bureau of Statistics explained . Among the 25,422,788 people that the census counted, 43,220 respondents chose nonbinary. But this “did not yield meaningful data,” the bureau later acknowledged, because the respondents hadn’t agreed upon a definition of nonbinary . Among the small number of respondents who selected nonbinary and explained why, “a very small number” indicated that they were intersex; “a small number” noted their sexual orientation; and three-fifths listed a gender identity. The bureau found the data unusable “to estimate the prevalence of any specific group.” The 2026 census will ask about sex and gender separately. A 2024 study from JAMA Ophthalmology reviewed pivotal clinical trials in the field between 1995 and 2022. It sought to determine whether sex and gender were used correctly (relying on the National Institutes of Health definitions of sex as “a biological characteristic, reflected genetically by chromosomes and physiologically by sex hormones, internal reproductive organs, and external genitalia” and gender as “an aspect of identity that is self-determined and influenced by sociocultural and environmental factors”). The researchers found that in 85 trials, “over three-quarters applied sex and gender terminology incorrectly” and that “no trial reported how sex or gender were collected,” even though “sex and gender are gaining increasing recognition as important determinants of disease epidemiology, health outcomes, and health care disparities.” The authors concluded that the “policies of biomedical journals on sex and gender are incongruous and uncoordinated” in a way that hurts the field’s mission. In a 2023 interview with Time magazine, the soccer player Megan Rapinoe objected to barring trans women from playing on the same sports teams as biological females. “I see trans women as real women,” she declared. “What you’re saying automatically in the argument—you’re sort of telling on yourself already—is you don’t believe these people are women.” But her formulation elides the fact that women is used variably, sometimes to signify sex and sometimes to signify gender. Many proponents of segregating sports by sex do not reject the gender identity of trans women. For example, in the prominent case of Lia Thomas, a trans woman who, controversially, swam on the women’s team at the University of Pennsylvania, 16 teammates sent a letter to Penn that stated, “We fully support Lia Thomas in her decision to affirm her gender identity and to transition from a man to a woman. Lia has every right to live her life authentically. However, we also recognize that when it comes to sports competition, that the biology of sex is a separate issue from someone’s gender identity.” Only by distinguishing between sex and gender can we distinguish between two different viewpoints: that sports leagues should reject a trans person’s account of their own gender, or that gender is irrelevant to this debate and sex alone should govern policy around eligibility to play. Different ideological groups will continue deploying language that best suits their ends. But we all ought to value terms that are accurate and aid mutual understanding. Clarity is best advanced by using sex to refer to biology––and, when appropriate, to specify whether the particular trait relevant to a given discussion concerns gametes, chromosomes, hormones, anatomy, or some combination. In contrast, gender should be used to refer to matters that are socially constructed––and concepts such as gender norms , gender identity , and gender expression should be used to distinguish different conceptions of gender from one another. If and when disputes arise about whether we’re referring to sex or gender or a mix, speakers should explain why they chose a given term and what precisely they mean by it. These usage conventions can’t tell us who belongs on what sports team or what is required or forbidden under antidiscrimination law, nor can it settle any number of other debates. But they can help us all better understand and engage in them.

items.title: Why the Middle East war still convulses the oil market – Report
items.description: After more than five months of conflict, oil markets continue to surge and tumble over the latest developments in the US-Iran clash, including President Donald Trump’s shifting pronouncements. What is behind the market’s volatility? – The ‘shock’ of Hormuz – While the potential vulnerability of the Strait of Hormuz has long been viewed as a risk, oil markets have still been caught off guard by Iran’s ability to largely close the crucial waterway. “What really shakes the market are surprises… and the Hormuz closure was a shock,” said Jim Burkhard, head of global energy crude oil research at S&P Global. Brent oil prices surged more than 13 percent in the immediate aftermath of the US-Israeli siege against Iran on February 28. Since that time, prices have been jolted in both directions as the conflict has dragged on. “Number one, it’s the complete unexpectedness, unfamiliarity with what we are seeing,” Bob McNally, president of the Rapidian Energy Group and a former White House energy advisor to George W. Bush, said of the unprecedented curtailment of the Strait. “There was this perception that the US would never allow it to happen,” McNally added. About 20 million barrels per day of crude traverse the Strait, roughly a quarter of global oil demand, making the current supply shock “the biggest disruption in history,” according to McNally. Subsequent events have jerked prices in both directions. Markets were unnerved by the US move to blockade Iran’s ports, but subsequently buoyed by a June 17 agreement between the United States and Iran to cease hostilities. – An imminent resolution? – While the conflict has boosted prices overall, international benchmark Brent oil has averaged $94 a barrel since the start of the fighting, well below the $150-per-barrel level seen by some experts as possible. One explanation is the market’s response to Trump, who has issued contradictory statements but has often described a Hormuz resolution as within striking distance. Such statements have helped keep crude prices from rising more. “The market believes and still believes that this crisis can and will end soon,” McNally said. Optimistic statements by the president and other Trump administration figures like Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have often sent oil prices sharply lower, posing peril to traders on the wrong side. “The oil market has sort of burned the bulls so many times you just don’t have bulls willing to go in and trade,” McNally said. “So all you have is people who are trading, especially these algorithmic traders who are just trading on headlines.” The Hormuz closure has lowered volumes by about 12.6 million barrels per day, according to JPMorgan Chase analysts. Some of this has been blunted by lower crude imports from China, while releases from commercial and government inventories have also offset the effects of lost supply. In March, the International Energy Agency announced member governments would release 400 million barrels of oil, the largest emergency stock release in history. The United States, Canada and Brazil have been among the countries increasing output. Middle East producers have maneuvered some shipments away from the Strait. For example, Saudi Arabia shifted crude exports to the Red Sea, but that avenue has also been compromised by attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels. – Not just oil – While the fluctuations of crude prices generate most of the headlines, analysts have also highlighted the stresses on refined products, including gasoline. “The most pressure in the world today is on refined products because there is generally enough crude oil out there right now, but there’s not enough refining capacity,” Burkhard said. Diesel prices have doubled compared with February, while gasoline prices are up about 50 percent. The Middle East conflict has also sidelined key energy infrastructure due to attacks, including some refinery capacity. Energy experts also point to Russian refinery outages due to attacks from Ukraine in that war. Continued robust demand for petroleum products has led to a historic surge in refinery profit margins, resulting in huge earnings windfalls for large oil companies in the second quarter. The post Why the Middle East war still convulses the oil market – Report appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Cyberbullying : When social media becomes a tool for public humiliation
items.description: A person can make one mistake in front of twenty people and survive the embarrassment. Make that same mistake in front of a smartphone camera, however, and the story can become very different. Within seconds, the video can move from one phone to another. Then it appears on WhatsApp. Someone posts it on TikTok. Another person uploads it to Facebook or X. A caption is added. The comments begin. People laugh. People insult. People share. People create memes. And before the person at the centre of the video even understands what is happening, a private moment of embarrassment has become a public spectacle. This is the frightening reality of cyberbullying in the digital age. Social media has revolutionised communication. Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X, WhatsApp and other platforms have made it possible for people to communicate, learn, advertise businesses, build careers and express themselves to audiences far beyond their immediate communities. But the same technology that gives people a voice can also give cruelty a microphone. The same smartphone that captures memories can capture someone’s most vulnerable moment. And the same “share” button that spreads useful information can spread humiliation to thousands of people. Cyberbullying is the deliberate use of digital platforms to insult, threaten, harass, intimidate, embarrass, expose or humiliate another person. It can happen through comments, private messages, group chats, photographs, videos, memes, fake accounts, edited content, false accusations and the unauthorised sharing of personal information. It can target almost anyone. A child. A university student. A worker. A public figure. A person with a disability. A person struggling financially. Someone who made a mistake. Or simply someone who looks, speaks or thinks differently. The frightening part is that cyberbullying is increasingly being disguised as entertainment. We call it a joke. We call it content. We call it “cruise.” We say, “It is just social media.” But for the person being humiliated, it is not “just social media.” It is their face. Their voice. Their reputation. Their confidence. Their dignity. Their life. When someone’s mistake becomes everybody’s entertainment One of the clearest examples is the mocking of people who make mistakes while speaking. Imagine a university student standing before a class to give a presentation. They are nervous. Their hands may shake. Their voice may tremble. They may mispronounce a few words. They may forget a sentence. These things happen. Public speaking is a skill that develops with practice. Yet instead of receiving encouragement or respectful correction, someone may secretly record the presentation. The video is uploaded. A funny caption is added. The student’s pronunciation becomes the subject of jokes. People who have never met the student begin laughing at them. Some may even tag friends and encourage them to watch. The student may return to class the next day knowing that hundreds or thousands of people have seen the video. The lesson is no longer about the presentation. It becomes about humiliation. And the next time that student is asked to speak publicly, they may remember what happened. They may become afraid to participate. They may begin questioning their intelligence. They may decide that silence is safer than making another mistake. That is how cyberbullying can steal something that cannot easily be measured: confidence. Not everything that is funny is harmless We need to have an uncomfortable conversation about humour. Humour is part of human life. People laugh. People joke. Friends tease each other. There is nothing inherently wrong with comedy. The problem begins when the joke depends on another person’s humiliation. If one person is laughing and another is suffering, we should question whether it is really a joke. The fact that thousands of people find something funny does not make it harmless. Popularity does not turn cruelty into kindness. Virality does not make humiliation acceptable. And a laughing emoji does not erase the pain caused by an insult. The culture of “content” is making things worse The competition for views, likes, followers and shares has created a digital environment where almost anything can become content. Someone falls. Record it. Someone cries. Record it. Someone is arguing. Record it. Someone makes a mistake. Record it. Someone is embarrassed. Record it. The camera often comes out before compassion does. This should concern us. We are becoming a society in which witnessing another person’s vulnerable moment can trigger the instinct to document it rather than help. Instead of asking, “Are you okay?”, someone may ask, “Can I post this?” Instead of helping a person who has fallen, another person may first reach for a phone. Instead of protecting someone’s dignity, we sometimes protect the opportunity for views. Technology did not create cruelty, but it has made cruelty easier to distribute. The crowd behind the screen Cyberbullying is rarely the work of one person alone. Sometimes one individual creates the original harmful post, but hundreds or thousands of people participate by sharing it. This is where bystanders become important. The person who created the video may have started the humiliation. But the people who shared it gave the humiliation wings. The person who wrote the insulting caption started the attack. But the people who liked and reposted it helped amplify it. We therefore need to stop thinking that only the original poster is responsible for online harm. Every user has a choice. You can share. You can comment. You can report. You can ignore. Or you can stop the spread. Anonymity can remove accountability Another problem is the use of anonymous and fake accounts. Some people hide behind usernames and profile pictures to say things they would never have the courage to say publicly. They insult people’s bodies. They attack their families. They spread rumours. They threaten people. They make sexualised comments. They destroy reputations. Because they believe they cannot be identified, they behave as though there are no consequences. But anonymity does not make cruelty less harmful. A victim still experiences the damage whether or not they know the identity of the person responsible. This is why online accountability matters. Cyberbullying can become more dangerous than a joke Online harassment can also move beyond insults. It can involve threats, impersonation, spreading false information, exposing private conversations, sharing personal information without permission and distributing intimate or embarrassing material. These actions can have serious consequences. A person’s reputation can be damaged. Relationships can collapse. Employment opportunities can be affected. Academic life can be disrupted. A victim may become afraid to leave home or interact socially. The internet can make a victim feel as though there is nowhere to escape. Home may not feel safe because the messages are arriving on their phone. School may not feel safe because classmates have seen the content. Work may not feel safe because colleagues have shared it. Even sleep can become difficult because the victim keeps checking what people are saying. That is not harmless entertainment. The victim is often blamed One of the most disturbing reactions to cyberbullying is victim-blaming. When a private photograph is leaked, people may ask why the victim took the photograph. When someone is mocked for their appearance, people may tell them to change. When someone is insulted online, people may say they should simply ignore it. When an embarrassing video spreads, people may ask why the person behaved that way in the first place. These responses shift responsibility from the person doing the harm to the person being harmed. We must reject that thinking. Someone’s mistake does not give others permission to humiliate them. Someone’s appearance does not justify abuse. Someone’s private photograph does not give others the right to distribute it. Someone’s opinion does not make them deserving of threats. The responsibility for abusive behaviour belongs to the person choosing to engage in it. Young people need protection, but also education Children and young people are particularly vulnerable because social media is deeply connected to their social lives. For many young people, being excluded from an online group can feel like being excluded from their entire social world. A cruel comment from one person can quickly become a group attack. A private disagreement can become public. A rumour can travel through an entire school before a teacher even knows it exists. Parents therefore need to understand the digital environments their children inhabit. Schools and universities should not wait until a serious incident occurs before discussing cyberbullying. Students should be taught about digital citizenship, privacy, consent, responsible sharing and online consequences. They should also know how and where to seek help. The goal should not be to frighten young people away from technology. The goal should be to teach them how to use it responsibly. Universities have a responsibility Universities are important spaces for addressing this issue because students spend a significant part of their lives communicating digitally. A student may be mocked in a class WhatsApp group. A lecturer’s presentation may be secretly recorded. A student’s photograph may be circulated without consent. A private disagreement may become a campus-wide social media issue. Institutions should therefore create clear policies and reporting mechanisms for serious online harassment. Students should know who they can approach. Cases involving threats, harassment or serious reputational harm should not simply be dismissed as “students being students.” Young adults also deserve protection from harmful digital behaviour. Social media companies cannot escape responsibility The platforms themselves also have a responsibility. Social media companies benefit from the enormous amount of content users create. They must therefore continue developing effective systems for reporting harassment, threats, impersonation and harmful content. Users should have accessible privacy controls. Reporting mechanisms should be understandable. Repeated abusive behaviour should receive appropriate attention. The answer cannot be to place the entire burden on victims. A victim who is being attacked by hundreds of accounts cannot realistically respond to every comment individually. Technology created the scale of the problem. Technology must also be part of the solution. But the biggest change must happen in us Ultimately, however, no algorithm can replace basic human decency. We must decide what kind of internet culture we want. Do we want a digital environment where people are afraid to speak because every mistake could become viral? Do we want young people to grow up believing that humiliation is entertainment? Do we want smartphones to become tools for documenting people’s pain instead of helping them? Or do we want social media to be a space for learning, creativity, connection and responsible expression? The answer depends partly on the choices we make every day. Every share contributes to the culture. Every comment contributes to the culture. Every like contributes to the culture. Every time we refuse to participate, we also contribute to the culture. We need to change what we reward There is a reason humiliating content spreads so quickly. It attracts attention. And attention has become a form of currency online. The more outrageous the content, the more reactions it may receive. The more embarrassing the moment, the more people may want to watch. This creates an uncomfortable incentive structure. If cruelty brings views, some people will produce cruelty. If humiliation brings followers, some people will pursue humiliation. If insults generate engagement, some people will continue insulting others. We therefore need to become more intentional about what we reward with our attention. Not everything that goes viral deserves to be consumed. Not everything that is trending deserves a share. And not everything that makes us laugh deserves to remain online. Sometimes the most responsible thing a social media user can do is simply not participate. Correction should not become humiliation There is nothing wrong with correcting mistakes. If someone mispronounces a word, teach them. If someone uses incorrect grammar, correct them respectfully. If someone shares false information, provide accurate information. If someone expresses an unpopular opinion, challenge the argument rather than attacking the person. The purpose of correction should be improvement. When correction becomes humiliation, learning disappears. A person who is publicly mocked for making a mistake may become afraid to make another attempt. That does not make society better. It creates people who are afraid to speak. And a society in which people are afraid to speak, ask questions and learn from mistakes is not a healthy society. What should victims do? Victims of cyberbullying should not be made to feel that they caused the abuse. Where possible, they should avoid engaging endlessly with abusive accounts. They can preserve evidence of serious harassment, block abusive users and use platform reporting tools. Where threats or serious harassment are involved, appropriate authorities or trusted support systems should be considered. Most importantly, victims should not suffer in isolation. A person who is being publicly humiliated needs support, not another lecture about what they should have done differently. Friends and family can make an enormous difference simply by listening and standing with the person. The bystander has power We often talk about bullies and victims. But there is another important group: the audience. The audience decides whether harmful content dies quickly or travels widely. The audience decides whether an insult receives encouragement or silence. The audience decides whether a person’s embarrassment becomes a national joke or disappears into the internet. This means that every social media user has some responsibility. We do not have to become heroes. Sometimes we simply need to refuse to participate. Do not share the humiliating video. Do not add the insulting comment. Do not forward the private photograph. Do not laugh at someone’s pain simply because everyone else is laughing. Do not turn another person’s worst moment into your entertainment. Social media should not punish people for being human People will make mistakes. They will stumble over words. They will forget things. They will dress differently. They will express unpopular opinions. They will sometimes behave awkwardly. They will fail. They will learn. They will grow. That is what being human means. If every mistake is recorded and every weakness is exposed, we create a society where people are constantly performing instead of genuinely living. Everyone becomes afraid of being watched. Everyone becomes afraid of being judged. Everyone becomes afraid that one bad moment could define them forever. That is not freedom. That is digital fear. We must build a culture where people can make mistakes without becoming targets. The conversation must become national Cyberbullying should no longer be treated as merely a social media problem. It intersects with education, mental wellbeing, privacy, child protection, digital literacy, human dignity and responsible citizenship. Parents must talk about it. Schools must teach about it. Universities must address it. Media organisations must discuss it. Influencers must model responsible behaviour. Technology companies must strengthen protections. And social media users must understand that their actions have consequences. The solution begins with a simple principle: Just because you can post something does not mean you should. Technology gives us the ability to reach millions. It does not give us the right to destroy someone’s dignity. Before posting, commenting, recording or sharing, we should pause and ask: Is this true? Is this necessary? Is this respectful? Would I want this done to me? And if the answer is no, perhaps the best button to press is not “share.” It is “delete.” Because behind every username is a human being. Behind every photograph is a person. Behind every embarrassing video is someone who may be trying desperately to forget what happened. The internet may move quickly, but human emotions do not always heal at the same speed. A cruel comment may take five seconds to write. A humiliating video may take ten seconds to upload. A share may take one second. But the damage can last for years. So the next time we see someone being mocked online, let us not ask only, “Is this funny?” Let us ask: “What if this were me?” Social media should be a place where people connect, learn, create and express themselves—not a digital courtroom where ordinary human mistakes are punished before millions of spectators. We cannot control everything that appears on the internet. But we can control what we contribute to it. And perhaps the most powerful way to fight cyberbullying is to remember something that technology can never erase: There is a human being behind the screen. Do not turn someone’s mistake into your entertainment. Do not turn their pain into your content. And do not let the click of a button become the beginning of someone’s suffering.

Le parti a par ailleurs exigé la levée de ce qu'il qualifie « d'isolement imposé par la ministre de la Justice », tout en réaffirmant le droit de Rached Ghannouchi de recevoir les visites de ses avocats et de sa famille, conformément à la loi. items.title: Tinubu approves offshore reform to unlock $50bn investment
items.description: President Bola Tinubu has approved a landmark reform aimed at unlocking up to 50 billion dollars in deep offshore investment and reviving stalled offshore projects. The reform replaces project-by-project negotiations with a transparent, rules-based investment framework designed to attract long-term capital into Nigeria’s offshore oil and gas sector. This is contained in a statement issued by Presidential Spokesperson, Mr Bayo Onanuga, on Tuesday in Abuja. According to the Presidency, the framework will support a new generation of deep offshore developments, beginning with the approximately 10 billion dollars Bonga South West project. It is also expected to strengthen Nigeria’s competitiveness in attracting globally mobile investment capital. The decision follows Tinubu’s engagement with Shell plc Chief Executive Officer, Mr Wael Sawan, during which measures to unlock Nigeria’s deep offshore investment pipeline were discussed. Rather than adopting project-specific solutions, the Federal Government developed a comprehensive framework applicable to multiple qualifying developments. The framework, established through the Deep Offshore Oil and Gas Projects Incentives (Tax Remission) Order, 2026, introduces transparent eligibility criteria and clear implementation processes. It also provides greater certainty for investors while safeguarding long-term national value. The approval enables NNPC Ltd. , as the government’s nominated counterparty under Production Sharing Contracts, to proceed with amendments required to implement the framework. Tinubu commended the Federal Ministries of Justice, Finance and Petroleum Resources, as well as the Nigeria Revenue Service, NNPC Ltd. and other stakeholders for their contributions. He also praised the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission, the Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board, and investing partners for helping to shape the framework. “The countries that attract long-term investment are not necessarily those with the greatest natural resources. “They are the ones that provide the greatest certainty. “This reform reflects our determination to build an investment environment defined by clear rules, strong institutions and enduring partnerships. “We are creating the conditions for capital to flow, for Nigerian businesses to grow, for our people to prosper and for our natural resources to deliver lasting national value,” Tinubu said. Mrs Olu Verheijen, Special Adviser to the President on Energy, said the reform places strong emphasis on strengthening Nigerian industrial capacity. “Projects qualifying under the framework will maximise execution within Nigeria wherever commercially and technically feasible. “The objective is not only to increase investment and production, but also to create skilled jobs, deepen local supply chains and position Nigeria as Africa’s regional hub for deep offshore project execution,” she said.
